**Spearman Correlation Analysis for Multicollinearity Reduction**

**Goal:** Identify which of the \~257 variables are most similar to each other, so we can reduce covariate redundancy

```{r}
## 1. Set up

# Packages
required_packages <- c("corrplot", "reshape2", "caret", "dplyr", "Hmisc")
new_packages <- required_packages[!(required_packages %in% installed.packages()[,"Package"])]
if(length(new_packages)) install.packages(new_packages, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")

library(corrplot)
library(reshape2)
library(caret)
library(dplyr)
library(Hmisc)

# Load & Prep Data
df <- read.csv("/Users/marileekarinshak/MexicoProject/harris-week7/data/processed/Covariates/merged_covariates.csv")

## Columns to exclude from correlation (IDs, labels, dates, etc.)
## Edit this vector to match your actual non-numeric / non-variable columns
id_cols <- c("CVEGEO","NOMGEO")

## Keep only numeric columns (Spearman correlation requires numeric data)
num_df <- df %>%
  select(-any_of(id_cols)) %>%
  select(where(is.numeric))

cat("Number of numeric-type columns before filtering:", ncol(num_df), "\n")
```

```{r}

## 1.5 Filtering out columns that are numeric but not continuous

unique_value_threshold <- 5   # columns with <= this many unique values are treated as categorical/binary

col_diagnostics <- data.frame(
  column = names(num_df),
  n_unique = sapply(num_df, function(x) length(unique(na.omit(x)))),
  is_integer_type = sapply(num_df, is.integer),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

## Flag columns as "likely categorical" if they have few unique values
## (covers binary 0/1 flags, Likert scales, category codes, etc.)
low_unique_cols <- col_diagnostics$column[col_diagnostics$n_unique <= unique_value_threshold]

if(length(low_unique_cols) > 0){
  cat("\nExcluding", length(low_unique_cols), "columns with <=", unique_value_threshold,
      "unique values (likely binary/categorical, not continuous):\n")
  print(low_unique_cols)
  num_df <- num_df %>% select(-all_of(low_unique_cols))
}

## Also drop any date/datetime/POSIX columns that slipped through
date_cols <- names(num_df)[sapply(num_df, function(x) inherits(x, c("Date", "POSIXct", "POSIXt")))]
if(length(date_cols) > 0){
  cat("\nExcluding date/time columns:", paste(date_cols, collapse = ", "), "\n")
  num_df <- num_df %>% select(-all_of(date_cols))
}

cat("\nNumber of continuous variables remaining for correlation analysis:", ncol(num_df), "\n")
 
## Drop zero-variance columns (constant columns break correlation)
zero_var_cols <- names(num_df)[sapply(num_df, function(x) sd(x, na.rm = TRUE) == 0)]
if(length(zero_var_cols) > 0){
  cat("Dropping zero-variance columns:", paste(zero_var_cols, collapse = ", "), "\n")
  num_df <- num_df %>% select(-all_of(zero_var_cols))
}
```

```{r}
## 2. Compute correlation matrices (Spearman = primary, Pearson = comparison)

spearman_result <- rcorr(as.matrix(num_df), type = "spearman")
corr_matrix   <- spearman_result$r  
p_matrix      <- spearman_result$P

pearson_result  <- rcorr(as.matrix(num_df), type = "pearson")
pearson_matrix  <- pearson_result$r
pearson_p       <- pearson_result$P

## 3. Turn the matrix into a long "pairs" table 
## This output gives a ranked list of which variable pairs are most redundant with each other.

get_pairs_table <- function(corr_matrix, p_matrix){
  corr_matrix[upper.tri(corr_matrix, diag = TRUE)] <- NA
  p_matrix[upper.tri(p_matrix, diag = TRUE)] <- NA
  
  corr_long <- melt(corr_matrix, na.rm = TRUE, varnames = c("Var1", "Var2"), value.name = "correlation")
  p_long    <- melt(p_matrix,    na.rm = TRUE, varnames = c("Var1", "Var2"), value.name = "p_value")
  
  merged <- merge(corr_long, p_long, by = c("Var1", "Var2"))
  merged$abs_correlation <- abs(merged$correlation)
  merged <- merged[order(-merged$abs_correlation), ]
  rownames(merged) <- NULL
  merged
}

pairs_table         <- get_pairs_table(corr_matrix, p_matrix)          # Spearman (primary)
pairs_table_pearson <- get_pairs_table(pearson_matrix, pearson_p)      # Pearson (comparison)

## Merge the two so you can see, side by side, where the methods agree/disagree
comparison_table <- merge(
  pairs_table[, c("Var1","Var2","correlation")],
  pairs_table_pearson[, c("Var1","Var2","correlation")],
  by = c("Var1","Var2"),
  suffixes = c("_spearman", "_pearson")
)
comparison_table$abs_diff <- abs(comparison_table$correlation_spearman - comparison_table$correlation_pearson)
comparison_table <- comparison_table[order(-comparison_table$abs_diff), ]

cat("\nTop 15 pairs where Spearman and Pearson disagree the most\n")
cat("(large gaps usually mean a nonlinear-but-monotonic relationship, or outlier-driven Pearson distortion):\n")

print(head(comparison_table, 15))
```

```{r}
## 4. Flag pairs that appear too similar
## 0.7-0.8 is a common rule-of-thumb cutoff for concerning multicollinearity (but adjust threshold based on our needs)

threshold <- 0.7

high_corr_pairs <- pairs_table %>%
  filter(abs_correlation >= threshold)

cat("\nNumber of variable pairs with |Spearman| >=", threshold, ":", nrow(high_corr_pairs), "\n")

cat("Top 20 most correlated pairs (Spearman):\n")

print(head(pairs_table, 20))
```

```{r}
## 5. Suggest which columns to DROP to reduce multicollinearity 
## caret::findCorrelation uses a greedy algorithm: for each pair above
## the cutoff, it removes the variable with the larger mean absolute
## correlation to all other variables (i.e., the more "redundant" one
## overall), trying to keep the max number of usable variables.

cor_for_caret <- cor(num_df, use = "pairwise.complete.obs", method = "spearman")

# handle any remaining NAs (can occur if a variable pair never overlaps)
cor_for_caret[is.na(cor_for_caret)] <- 0

drop_indices <- findCorrelation(cor_for_caret, cutoff = threshold, names = TRUE, exact = TRUE)

cat("\nSuggested columns to DROP (", length(drop_indices), " of ", ncol(num_df), "):\n", sep = "")
print(drop_indices)

kept_vars <- setdiff(colnames(num_df), drop_indices)
cat("\nSuggested columns to KEEP (", length(kept_vars), " of ", ncol(num_df), "):\n", sep = "")
print(kept_vars)

```

```{r}
# 6. Group variables into correlation "clusters" 
## This helps you see WHICH variables are redundant with which —
## useful if you want to manually pick one representative per cluster
## rather than trust the automated drop list.

dist_matrix <- as.dist(1 - abs(cor_for_caret))
hc <- hclust(dist_matrix, method = "average")

## Cut the tree so that within-cluster correlation is >= threshold
## (height = 1 - threshold on this distance scale)
cluster_assignments <- cutree(hc, h = 1 - threshold)

cluster_table <- data.frame(
  variable = names(cluster_assignments),
  cluster  = cluster_assignments
) %>%
  arrange(cluster)

cat("\nNumber of clusters of similar variables:", length(unique(cluster_assignments)), "\n")

## Show clusters that contain more than one variable (i.e., actual redundancy groups)
redundant_clusters <- cluster_table %>%
  group_by(cluster) %>%
  filter(n() > 1) %>%
  arrange(cluster)

cat("\nClusters with 2+ similar variables (candidates for keeping just 1 each):\n")
print(redundant_clusters, n = 100)
```

```{r}
OUT_VIS   <- "/Users/marileekarinshak/MexicoProject/harris-week7/data/processed/StateCap/municipality_capital_distances.csv"


# ---- 7. Visualizations ----
dir.create("outputs", showWarnings = FALSE)

## 7a. Full heatmap (only readable if you zoom into the saved PNG,
## since 257 variables is a lot to show at once)
png("outputs/correlation_heatmap_full.png", width = 4000, height = 4000, res = 300)
corrplot(corr_matrix,
         method = "color",
         type = "upper",
         order = "hclust",     # groups similar variables together visually
         tl.cex = 0.4,         # shrink text so labels don't overlap
         tl.col = "black",
         diag = FALSE)
dev.off()

## 7b. Smaller heatmap showing ONLY the high-correlation pairs' variables
## (much easier to actually read)
vars_in_high_pairs <- unique(c(high_corr_pairs$Var1, high_corr_pairs$Var2))

if(length(vars_in_high_pairs) > 1){
  png("outputs/correlation_heatmap_highcorr_only.png", width = 3000, height = 3000, res = 300)
  corrplot(corr_matrix[vars_in_high_pairs, vars_in_high_pairs],
           method = "color",
           type = "upper",
           order = "hclust",
           tl.cex = 0.7,
           tl.col = "black",
           addCoef.col = "black",  # show actual correlation values
           number.cex = 0.5,
           diag = FALSE)
  dev.off()
}

## 7c. Dendrogram showing variable clustering
png("outputs/variable_clustering_dendrogram.png", width = 4000, height = 2000, res = 300)
plot(hc, cex = 0.5, main = "Variable Similarity Clustering (1 - |Spearman rho|)",
     xlab = "", sub = "")
abline(h = 1 - threshold, col = "red", lty = 2)
dev.off()
```

```{r}

## ---- 8. Save all tables to CSV ----
write.csv(pairs_table, "outputs/all_pairwise_correlations_spearman.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(pairs_table_pearson, "outputs/all_pairwise_correlations_pearson.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(comparison_table, "outputs/spearman_vs_pearson_comparison.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(high_corr_pairs, "outputs/high_correlation_pairs.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(cluster_table, "outputs/variable_clusters.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(data.frame(kept_variable = kept_vars), "outputs/suggested_covariates_to_keep.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(data.frame(dropped_variable = drop_indices), "outputs/suggested_covariates_to_drop.csv", row.names = FALSE)

cat("\n============================================================\n")
cat("DONE. Check the 'outputs' folder for:\n")
cat(" - all_pairwise_correlations_spearman.csv  (every pair, ranked by |rho| -- PRIMARY)\n")
cat(" - all_pairwise_correlations_pearson.csv   (every pair, Pearson, for comparison)\n")
cat(" - spearman_vs_pearson_comparison.csv      (pairs where the two methods disagree most)\n")
cat(" - high_correlation_pairs.csv              (Spearman pairs above threshold =", threshold, ")\n")
cat(" - variable_clusters.csv                   (which variables group together, Spearman-based)\n")
cat(" - suggested_covariates_to_keep.csv        (caret's recommended set, Spearman-based)\n")
cat(" - suggested_covariates_to_drop.csv        (caret's recommended drops, Spearman-based)\n")
cat(" - correlation_heatmap_full.png            (all variables, Spearman, ordered by similarity)\n")
cat(" - correlation_heatmap_highcorr_only.png   (just the problematic ones, readable)\n")
cat(" - variable_clustering_dendrogram.png      (visual tree of similar variables)\n")
cat("============================================================\n")
```
